### D-EV-INQUIRY-GATE — may a guest create an event for a venue that cannot see it

plan.md:21117

**Why it is open**

The public enquiry write is ungated. A guest can create an event row for a store whose admin surface answers
**404** — a confirmation for a booking the venue can never see.
**It was left for a ruling rather than fixed, and that was the right call**, by the same lane that gated
accept and decline. Those two had nothing recorded against them at all; the payment callback was left alone
on purpose and the reason was written down. This one is a product call about the funnel, not a defect.

**The options**

- `refuse-the-write`
  - **pro:** no guest ever receives a confirmation for a booking the venue can never see, and the refusal is one gate on one write
  - **con:** closes the front door on the thing that plausibly sells the module, since the enquiry form may be how a venue discovers Events at all
- `hide-the-form`
  - **pro:** keeps the write reachable for anyone who already has the link while removing the路 by which a stranger reaches an un-opted venue
  - **con:** a link outlives the page, so the confirmation-for-nothing case survives for anyone who bookmarked or was sent one
- `leave-it-open-and-say-so`
  - **pro:** honest about a deliberate posture, and matches the payment callback, which the same lane left ungated on purpose because gating it would strand in-flight money
  - **con:** the venue-side silence stays, and the plan carries a documented hole rather than a closed one

**No recommendation is recorded** for this one.

### D-ACTOR-KIND-FOR-A-TILL-OPERATOR — what the system says a till operator is

plan.md:21134

**Why it is open**

**Two lanes change one interface on different bases and neither can see the other.** One makes the actor pair
a **required, undefaulted** parameter on both release members; the other adds a third member for the till,
**stamped with a POS operator — for which the actor-kind enum has no correct value.**
**Confirmed by a merge actually performed rather than reasoned about, 2026-08-06.** The collision is real and
has an offender neither branch shows alone: the tip's till tender stamp names no actor kind, and the
vocabulary available has no correct value for a till operator.
**That is what makes this a ruling and not a fix. It is not that a call site forgot to pass a value — there
is no value to pass.** Adding one changes what the system says an actor *is*.

**The options**

- `add-a-pos-operator-kind`
  - **pro:** names the thing that actually happened, so a funded release stamped at a till is traceable to a person and C4 holds without a fiction
  - **con:** widens the actor vocabulary, which every existing consumer of that enum must then handle, and the enum is read on money-path writes across four modules
- `stamp-the-staff-kind`
  - **pro:** no vocabulary change, and a till operator is a staff member, so the value is not false
  - **con:** erases the distinction between a shift-scheduled action and a till action in the one record an auditor reads to tell them apart
- `make-the-till-member-actorless-and-refuse`
  - **pro:** keeps the interface honest by refusing what it cannot attribute, rather than attributing it wrongly
  - **con:** the till path is the one that closes the reachability gap, so refusing it leaves no operator able to make a credit sale at a till at all

**No recommendation is recorded** for this one.

If you do nothing: nothing moves — there is no default.

```
plan decide D-ACTOR-KIND-FOR-A-TILL-OPERATOR --choose add-a-pos-operator-kind|stamp-the-staff-kind|make-the-till-member-actorless-and-refuse --by @sven
```

### D-SPEC-L-PUBLISH-WRITES-ONE-OUTBOX-ROW — the plan contradicts what L-PUBLISH-WRITES-ONE-OUTBOX-ROW observed

plan.md:21154

**Why it is open**

**The lane was right and the exit was wrong.** *(Authored by the clerk from the lane's finding; the ruling is
the owner's.)*
**The two rows are siblings, not duplicates.** Different `Channel`, different `TargetReference`, different
`LogicalDedupeKey` — `InApp`/`<staffId>`/`…:inapp` and `Email`/an address/`…:email` — against one recipient row
and one inbox item. **The person receives one inbox entry and one e-mail.**
**Not two write paths either**: one loop over `WorkforceNotificationChannelPlan.Plan(...)`, emitting one command
per channel that can reach the recipient.
**The cause is a stale assertion, not a regression.** `f5305ced` (2026-08-01) replaced a hard-coded single
in-app command with the channel plan and updated all four fast-tier assertions. Its own commit message says
*"SQL tier not run."* `SchedulePublishSqlServerTests` is `Database=SqlServer`, so its count line was
**unreachable from every routine run and has read 1 for five days.**
**It is not a SQL Server behaviour.** Transliterating the test body to the SQLite fixture reproduces
`Expected 1 / Actual 2`, so the provider is irrelevant.
**No migration and no constraint are wanted.** A unique index on `LogicalDedupeKey` already exists and is
already satisfied — the keys differ by the channel suffix. Nor is this an idempotency question: the two
commands are not retries of each other.

**What it is blocking**

- L-PUBLISH-WRITES-ONE-OUTBOX-ROW — one publish produces one notification, not two (blocked)
- F-PUBLISH-DOUBLE-OUTBOX — the second outbox row is a sibling, and the assertion was stale · stays open while that lane waits

**The options**

- `assert-the-channel-set`
  - **pro:** the count becomes the exact channel set plus the address the external command is aimed at, so the assertion reds if a channel is dropped AND if one is added or reordered — the lane proved all three by mutation
  - **con:** a set assertion must be edited whenever a channel is legitimately added, which is a real edit rather than a silent pass
- `keep-the-count-at-one`
  - **pro:** simplest possible assertion, and it is what the exit already says
  - **con:** the lane's own M1 mutant shows this state IS "drop the external tier" — it deletes the e-mail that an invited, not-yet-claimed worker depends on, since the in-app adapter is a no-op and the inbox is unreachable until they claim
- `assert-one-row-per-planned-channel`
  - **pro:** tolerant of new channels without an edit, so it never blocks a legitimate addition
  - **con:** it cannot catch a channel silently disappearing, which is the actual risk here and the thing the SQL tier just caught

**No recommendation is recorded** for this one.

If you do nothing: nothing moves — there is no default.


### D-WF-CORRECTION-FLAG — whether the personalliste correction answers to a stage flag

plan.md:7036

**Why it is open**

**Raised by `L-WF-CORRECTION-PATH`, which built the write and then declined to choose its lever.**
The correction is behind **no** stage flag today. `WorkforceFeatureFlags.Withheld` records why, which keeps
`WorkforceFlagConsumptionTests`' "the two withheld keys gate nothing" true with no catalog change.
This is a Sven call because the two failure modes are not symmetric and neither is a code question. An
ungated write means one Workforce surface permanently outside the flag model. A gated one means a
configuration exists in which a venue silently stops keeping a register the law says it must keep.
If the ruling is `own-flag`, the honest execution is **both** halves — un-withhold the flag *and* extend
`WorkforceFlagCensus.Mutations`. This estate has counted eleven advertised-but-ungating flags; adding a
twelfth while ruling against them would be worse than leaving it ungated.
**Fable recommends `ungated`, and the built state already encodes the ruling with its legal argument at the
site.** The flag file withholds the personnel-list flag **precisely because § 8-5-6 makes recording a
rettelse part of keeping the register** — a flag that paused corrections *"would leave a venue holding a
register it knows is wrong and may not fix."*
**`own-flag` manufactures a configuration in which a venue silently stops keeping a statutory register.** The
census law survives because withheld-with-a-reason is the estate's established mechanism, with a Training
precedent and a probe already showing the route refuses on the module master only. **And the honest scope of
"every write has a lever" is preserved:** the module flag still fences it.

**What it is blocking**

- L-WF-STATUTORY-LAND — the four workforce lanes reach the branch the plan calls integration (blocked)

**The options**

- `ungated`
  - **pro:** bokforingsforskriften § 8-5-6 makes recording a rettelse part of keeping the register, so a lever that switches it off is a lever that switches off compliance
  - **con:** it becomes the only Workforce write answering to no stage flag, so "every write has a lever" stops being true and the census carries a permanent exemption
- `own-flag`
  - **pro:** restores the invariant that every write has a lever, and a venue not yet keeping the register digitally can keep the surface dark
  - **con:** a dark flag on a statutory correction path puts a venue out of compliance silently, and it needs a catalog change plus an extension to WorkforceFlagCensus.Mutations
- `reuse-clock`
  - **pro:** no catalog change, no census extension, ships as it stands
  - **con:** the lane measured this as wrong, because pausing the till clock is exactly when yesterday's window most needs correcting, so the lever would darken the path precisely when it is needed

Ruled: ungated 2026-08-05 by @sven

Reopen when: a legal reading holds that a venue may lawfully keep the register on paper while clocking digitally in this product

### D-WF-LINEAGE-PRODUCIBLE — whether a corrected personalliste entry shows what was corrected

plan.md:7372

**Why it is open**

**Raised by the Fable review of `L-WF-CORRECTION-PATH`, which ruled the statutory claim backed and then
named what is still missing from the document.**
The correction records **who** and **when**, and both render on screen and on the printed sheet as
*"Rettet av {actor} {date} {time}"*. The original row is retained and cannot be altered — verified in
two real layers, an EF guard and an AFTER UPDATE, DELETE trigger that throws 50017, both present in the
migration chain rather than merely claimed.
**But `BuildAsync` filters superseded rows out and no endpoint resolves `SupersedesEntryId`.** So the
sheet says a correction happened and by whom, and cannot say **what it changed**. The letter of § 8-5-6
is met. C6's standard is producibility, and by that standard this is half a document.
A second, smaller question rides along and is worth ruling in the same breath: **"hvem" prints as an
opaque Guid.** It is resolvable through the roster read, so it is producible in-product — but an
inspector reading paper sees a reference, not a person. Resolving it to a display name at render is a
join, not a register change.
**Fable recommends `screen-only`, and rules a rider in the same breath: resolve the actor to a display name at
render.** The register build filters superseded rows, and rows carry the supersession and actor references
**with nothing resolving either** — so the before-value is producible only from the database, **which fails
C6's standard even though § 8-5-6's letter is met.**
**Producibility is C6's test, not default printing.** An inspector reading *"Rettet av …"* on paper can ask,
and the product must then be able to produce the superseded row; printing it by default lengthens a statutory
sheet in a form **no inspector has asked for.** The name resolution is a join at render, not a register
change, and should not wait for a second decision cycle.

**The options**

- `screen-only`
  - **pro:** an inspector who asks can be shown the superseded row on screen without changing what the paper register is
  - **con:** the paper sheet remains half a document, and an inspection that starts from paper never learns a correction had a before
- `screen-and-paper`
  - **pro:** the printed register carries its own lineage, so the document is complete in the medium an inspector actually asks for
  - **con:** a sheet with struck-through history is longer and harder to read, and no one has asked for it
- `leave-as-is`
  - **pro:** the letter of § 8-5-6 is already met, who and when are both recorded and rendered
  - **con:** C6 asks whether the document can be produced, not whether the field exists, and the before-value is producible only from the database

Ruled: screen-only 2026-08-05 by @sven

Reopen when: Skatteetaten guidance or an actual kontroll requires the superseded values on the printed register itself

### D-MEALS-FINALIZE-OWNER — which surface owns the irreversible statement freeze

plan.md:9456

**Why it is open**

**Named by `L-MEALS-STATEMENT-SURFACE` when it returned `blocked` rather than dressing a partial as met,
and it is a decision the plan did not have.**
Two lanes were found binding the same irreversible freeze — recorded as `F-TWO-FINALIZE-CONTROLS`, caught
by a lane **watching the shared checkout go dirty under it**, not at a merge. Told to consume rather than
duplicate, it did: **it built no second finalize control and no second draft control.**
**The consequence is that its own exit became unreachable.** That exit names three stages walked in a
browser; a browser *control* walked one. Draft and finalize went through the API context, **labelled `API`
in their own step names inside the artifact** rather than presented as browser steps.
**The seam it took was one the sibling had drawn itself** — that lane's own client header records which
statement reads are *"deliberately still absent"*, and those are exactly the three this lane took. So the
family is now bound once per half, which is the outcome the flag wanted.
**What the walk did prove is not nothing**, and the structural fact under it is the reason this matters:
`MealsStatementLine` carries **no membership id and no user id at all** — there is nothing on the payload
to reconstruct the reference from, so printing it is a persistence claim rather than a rendering one. Two
browser mutants red it at the right steps, one proving the CSV assertion is not carried by the screen.
The lane's own recommendation is `both-with-one-link`, and it is the cheapest: **the page already reads
the query param.**
**Fable recommends `both-with-one-link`, and the surfaces already say so themselves.** The statements page
reads a run id from the query and auto-opens; its own header records **why the freeze must stay beside the
exception queue** — *"two controls for one irreversible act, on two screens, means an operator can find the
one that cannot tell them what is stopping it"* — and explicitly notes that whoever merges the two **owes that
one link.**
**The other surface is already composed into the candidate and carries no such link yet**, so this is
genuinely one link carrying the run id. Giving the freeze to the statements page alone would **detach an
irreversible act from the only surface that can name the row blocking it** — the named-refusal capability the
estate just built.

**What it is blocking**

- L-MEALS-STATEMENT-SURFACE — the month statement is reachable by a person (blocked)
- L-JOURNEY-MEALS — the Company Meals surface is walked end to end (blocked)

**The options**

- `close-owns-it`
  - the month-close surface keeps the freeze and the statements page links to it
  - **pro:** it is the only surface whose refusal names the exception blocking it, which needed a join of the queue against a count-only problem document
  - **con:** the three-stage walk stays impossible from one page until a link is added, so the exit that asked for it cannot be met as written
- `statements-owns-it`
  - move the freeze to the statements page and strip it from the close
  - **pro:** draft, finalize and export then live on one surface and the walk is one journey
  - **con:** the naming join moves with it or is lost, and losing it returns the estate to a refusal that says a count and names nothing
- `both-with-one-link`
  - close keeps the freeze, statements gains a link from the close carrying the run id
  - **pro:** the page already reads that query param, so this is one link and no second control
  - **con:** two surfaces still show statement state, and the operator has to know which one freezes

Ruled: both-with-one-link 2026-08-05 by @sven

Reopen when: operators are observed mis-locating the freeze in use, in which case consolidate onto the surface that can name what is blocking it

### D-CONFIRM-SIXTH-HEAD — an unreviewed sixth head sits above the merged confirm family

plan.md:17366

**Why it is open**

Found by the lane that merged the family, **by pairwise ancestry check rather than by reading the log** —
which is why nobody had seen it. A sixth true head sits two test-only commits above one of the five, with
its own measured receipt. **Neither the review nor the brief mentions it.**
**The lane did not merge it, and the restraint is the point.** Unlike the post-merge repair it did take —
which both the review and the brief had named — this one was never reviewed or trial-merged, so pulling it
in unilaterally would put unaudited code into a tree whose whole value is that somebody read across it.
It also left **two separate stopping points, each with its own receipt**, so the reviewed-scope merge can be
taken alone and the repair separately.
**Moot as of 2026-08-05, verified twice.** The sixth head is `lane/crypto-pin-byform` — two test-only commits
above the family head — and **it is already an ancestor of the backend tip**, landed through a different
composition entirely. The clerk confirmed the ancestry directly.
**So `merge-as-is` has already happened de facto, and `leave-it-out` is no longer available.** What remains is
a **retroactive review** of two test-only commits and retiring the superseded family ref. **The plan currently
says the opposite of what the object graph says**, which is the part worth correcting promptly: unreviewed
code is in the tip while the board reports it waiting.

**The options**

- `review-then-merge`
  - send the sixth head through the same review the other five had, then merge it
  - **pro:** it keeps the rule that made this family safe to compose — every head reviewed before it enters the tree
  - **con:** another review pass before the family can be called finished
- `merge-as-is`
  - take it on the strength of its own receipt
  - **pro:** it carries a measured receipt and is only two test-only commits
  - **con:** unaudited code enters a composed tree that was audited precisely because nobody could see across the family, which is the property the review bought
- `leave-it-out`
  - land the reviewed five and let the sixth ride its own lane later
  - **pro:** nothing unreviewed enters, and both merge points already have receipts so either can be taken alone
  - **con:** a head left outside a merged family is how this estate got a nine-deep stack in the first place

Ruled: merge-as-is 2026-08-06 by @sven

Reopen when: the retroactive review of the two test-only commits finds something, which is the only way code already in the tip becomes a question again

### D-INTEGRATION-FASTFORWARD — whether the integration branch moves onto the merged stack

plan.md:17400

**Why it is open**

Raised by `L-MIG-STACK-LAND`, which did the whole merge and then **stopped at the one act that is not
its own**: `feature/restaurant-modules` is unmoved and nothing was pushed. Its branch is a strict
descendant, so the landing is mechanically trivial — **the question is entirely about timing under 152
in-flight lanes**, which is a judgement about people rather than about git.
The merge itself is proven: all seven links in dependency order, fast tier green at **every** merge commit
rather than only the last, and the model snapshot clean at the tip — which is the check that matters,
since the snapshot auto-merged at three of the links.
**What is not proven is the SQL tier.** 584 tests were discovered at the tip and zero executed; the joins
are unverified on a real catalog. The one that matters is the last link, whose accounting-day index tests
**compile and have never run anywhere.**
**The blocker audit makes this the dominant decision on the board, 2026-08-03.** Its finding: **the root
cause of forty-seven open blockers is merge, not build.** The integration branch has not moved since
2026-08-02; every clearing branch measured is unmerged; 162 of 259 branches sit behind it.
So the queue is not forty-seven things to build. **Most of them are things to land**, and the ref not
moving is what keeps them looking like work.
**Measured 2026-08-04, and it changes what this decision is asking. Verified by the clerk, not taken on
report — a lane reported divergence and the numbers here are my own.**
**The branches have diverged. A fast-forward is not possible.** `integration/mig-stack-land` did not fall
behind the integration branch — it forked at `3579bbbc` and both sides have moved since, the integration
branch by 59 commits (eight merge lanes landed there today) and the stack by 34.
**So the question is no longer "does the integration branch fast-forward onto the stack".** It is whether
those 34 commits — which carry the whole W5 timesheet family and MIG-25/MIG-26 — are **merged into** the
integration branch, with everything a merge here implies: the seven hazards this program has catalogued,
a chain replay across a migration stack, and a tier re-run at the merge commit rather than inherited.
**Sharpened 2026-08-04 by `L-MEALS-IDEMPOTENCY-REFUSAL`, which measured what the 34 commits actually
contain rather than only how many there are:** they touch **only `Migrations/**`** — zero
`Services/Meals/**` files differ between the two branches.
That narrows the question usefully. The fork is not two divergent bodies of product code; it is a
**migration stack** on one side and 59 commits of merged module work on the other. So the risk in
reconciling is concentrated where this estate has been burned before — chain replay, an index that exists
in the model and not the chain, and the `AccountingSummaries` shape — rather than spread across the
services.
**Two lanes have already chosen the stack as their base** (`L-WF-TIMESHEET-RACE`, and its killed
predecessor independently) because it carries the family the integration branch does not. So work is
accumulating on **both** sides of a fork that nothing has yet reconciled.
This is not a recommendation — the ruling is Sven's. It is the measurement the ruling needs, and the
option names in this decision no longer describe the choice available.
**The premise under this decision's first option no longer holds, measured 2026-08-05, and the clerk verified
it independently.** This block says the branch is *"a strict descendant, so this is a fast-forward with nothing
to resolve"*. It is not. `integration/mig-stack-land` and `feature/restaurant-modules` have **diverged: 34
commits on the stack side, 59 on the integration side**, and `--is-ancestor` fails in **both** directions.
Confirmed a second way: `GrowthAuditWriter.cs` exists on the integration branch and is absent from the stack.
**This is not a stale-ref artefact.** The integration branch last moved at 2026-08-04T12:00:29, roughly fourteen
hours before the document that described the relationship was written.
**So `fast-forward-now` is not available as written.** Landing the stack is a **hand merge across a 739-line
ledger divergence with the MIG-22 collision inside it** — a different act, with a different risk, from the one
this option describes. The other two options are unaffected; what has changed is that the cheap one is not
cheap.
**The clerk passed the false version to Sven in a status report.** Recorded here rather than quietly amended,
because a decision offered with a wrong `pro` is worse than a decision not yet offered.
**Fable-reviewed 2026-08-05, and none of the three options survives measurement.** At the backend refs the
merge-base is `3579bbbc` with a **59/34 divergence and `--is-ancestor` false in both directions** — so
`fast-forward-now` and `fast-forward-after-the-walk` **describe an act that does not exist**, and
`leave-it-and-land-per-lane` is the pathology that built the stack in the first place. The reviewer's
recommendation is to re-author this as a **single authored merge lane, chain-replayed from empty and
tier-rerun at the merge commit.**
**A second falsehood sits inside this block, and the clerk verified it independently.** The 2026-08-04
sharpening says the 34 stack commits *"touch only `Migrations/**`"*. Measured at the same refs, the stack side
carries **126 files outside `Migrations/`** — the Workforce timesheet family, Margin waste, Tripletex,
accounting summaries, plus entities, enums and tests. **This is a real code merge, not a chain replay with
trimmings**, and only the narrower claim — no `Services/Meals/**` on the stack side — holds.
**It interlocks with the duplicate-MIG-21 decision**, whose collision lives *inside* this merge and has to be
resolved within it rather than before it.

**What it is blocking**

- L-WF-OPERATOR-UNIQUE — one operator cannot hold two live links (built)
- L-WF-CORRECTION-UNIQUE — two concurrent corrections cannot both append (blocked)
- L-GROWTH-AUDIT-INDEX — the growth audit indexes exist in production, not only in the model (blocked)

**The options**

- `fast-forward-now`
  - move `feature/restaurant-modules` onto the merged stack
  - **pro:** the merge is done, the branch is a strict descendant so this is a fast-forward with nothing to resolve, the fast tier was green at every one of the seven merge commits, and it stops the next migration author forking a chain that is nine deep and not an ancestor
  - **con:** it moves the reference under 152 in-flight lane branches, every one of which will find its base has moved
- `fast-forward-after-the-walk`
  - hold the ref until the standing worlds are walked and torn down
  - **pro:** fewer lanes in flight to disturb, and the freed memory lets the SQL tier prove the joins first
  - **con:** every hour it waits, more lanes branch from a base that is nine migrations behind the truth
- `leave-it-and-land-per-lane`
  - keep the integration branch where it is and merge each lane individually later
  - **pro:** no single disruptive move
  - **con:** it is what produced a nine-deep unmergeable stack in the first place
- `author-a-merge-lane`
  - one authored merge of the stack into the integration branch, chain-replayed from empty and tier-rerun at the merge commit
  - **pro:** it is the only option that describes something that can actually happen — the two sides diverge 59 against 34 with neither an ancestor of the other, so no fast-forward exists — and it treats the stack as what it is, a real code merge carrying 126 files outside Migrations
  - **con:** it is a genuine merge with conflicts to resolve, it serialises behind one author, and the duplicate-migration collision lives inside it and must be resolved there rather than before it

Ruled: author-a-merge-lane 2026-08-06 by @sven

Reopen when: the merge lane finds the two sides cannot be reconciled by a merge either, or the duplicate-migration collision inside it turns out to need resolving before the merge rather than within it

### D-MRG-CURATION-CONTENT — the ingredient list itself, in the file that is waiting for it

plan.md:17505

**Why it is open**

Raised by `L-MRG-STARTER-150`, which built the mechanism and **refused to invent the content**, exactly as
`author-the-list` intended. Five semicolon columns: `name;base_unit;yield;packs;notes`.
**Its most useful design choice is a guard against the one failure a 150-line paste makes easy and
expensive: a tail that never arrived.** The file declares its own row and yield counts, and the pins hold
the parsed list to them — because a truncated list has **no wrong row in it**, there are simply fewer of
them, and a blank yield column is legal, so neither can be caught by validating rows one at a time.
**A refused line is dropped, never served**, so a bad edit can neither put a wrong factor in front of a
venue nor take the ingredients endpoint down for one.

**What it is blocking**

- L-MRG-STARTER-150 — the starter library serves the approved curation, not sixteen items (built)
- F-MRG-ONBOARD-16 — a venue types its own ingredient library · stays open while that lane waits

**The options**

- `fill-the-csv`
  - edit `Services/Margin/margin-starter-ingredients.csv` in place and set its two counters
  - **pro:** the form is the file, it opens in Excel, its own header explains every column and both enforced rules, and the mechanism around it is built and mutation-proven — an evening's work with no question to ask anybody
  - **con:** it is your evening, and the yield column will validate but not yet cost anything
- `ship-the-sixteen`
  - leave the curation at sixteen and revisit after a pilot
  - **pro:** nothing to do, and the mechanism serves whatever is present
  - **con:** onboarding is this module's own stated kill risk and sixteen ingredients is not a library a venue did not have to type
- `seed-from-invoices`
  - build the library from a real venue's supplier lines instead
  - **pro:** names, units and pack sizes are already true for that venue
  - **con:** it needs the invoice ingest, which is itself waiting on `D-EHF-INVOICE-ACCESS`

Ruled: fill-the-csv 2026-08-05 by @sven

### D-TRAIN-RETENTION-BASIS — two questions the horizon needs answered, not one number

plan.md:17568

**Why it is open**

Raised by `L-MIG-TRAIN-DISPLAY-SNAPSHOT`, which **refused to build rather than pick a number because one
was needed.** The brief made the retention period the gate and named three permitted groundings; the lane
measured all three and all three fail.
**Two things must be ruled here, not one.** First, **what period on what authority**, given §13.5 forbids
asserting a statutory duration without counsel. Second, **what the horizon does at expiry** — lock, in
which case the defect stands and is merely dated; or delete, which needs a C1 exception written openly,
because the sweep must remove rows that the append-only guard and two triggers exist to protect.
The lane re-proved the underlying defect by execution rather than inheriting it: a completion written
under one name, the roster renamed, the pack re-read — **identical apart from the subject line, and the
old name survives nowhere in the reprint.**

**The options**

- `counsel-first`
  - get a period and its authority confirmed by counsel before any column ships
  - **pro:** it is what the module's own spec §13.5 demands in writing, and it is the only route that lets the pack name a duration without inventing one
  - **con:** it is external and slow, and the frozen-name defect stands until it returns
- `product-policy-no-statute`
  - set a documented product retention with expiry that DELETES, stated as policy and never as a legal duration
  - **pro:** §13.5 explicitly permits a documented product policy, so this is inside the spec rather than around it, and it gives the data a real end
  - **con:** the sweep must remove rows that GuardAppendOnly and two triggers protect, so it needs an explicit C1 exception written as an exception rather than smuggled in
- `lock-only-and-say-so`
  - freeze the name, set a keep-until lock with no deletion, and state on the pack that these records are retained indefinitely
  - **pro:** it is what the personalliste actually does today, so it is honest about the estate's real behaviour and needs no new mechanism
  - **con:** it does not close the erasure gap at all — it documents it, which is a different thing from curing it

Ruled: product-policy-no-statute 2026-08-05 by @sven

Reopen when: counsel returns with an actual statutory retention duty, which sets the period by that authority and may forbid deletion entirely

plan.md:17594

Raised by the spike on hand-back, and the finding is that **the invoices are not missing from the world,
only from the repository.** Your own message of 2026-07-28 says Casper sent invoices as ingredient-cost
examples. **The ruling that unparked this lane landed six days after the attachment arrived, and nothing
in the ruling moved the files.**
An exhaustive sweep — home, Downloads, Desktop, Documents, filename and full-text including inside PDFs —

connected to Tripletex through Okam.** Every connection insert outside onboarding is under the test
project, and the app's own consumer token is unconfigured — the settings type is bound in the composition
root and appears in neither appsettings file. So the probe is two credentials short, not one.
The spike also corrected the framing of the decision it came from. It could not test the pre-mandate
counter-argument empirically, but it established that **the sending obligation starts 1 January 2027** —
five months out. A STOP measured on today's mix carries a known expiry.
**Returned fail-spec 2026-08-03, and the return is the valuable part.** Both halves were already closed at
the base the brief sent it to, and **the second half's prescribed remedy would have broken the register**:
moving the journal id onto the delivery entry makes a credit sale non-refundable at the till, because the
return path refuses any original that is not a Sale and the refund modal calls straight through that field.
What it built instead is real and is held at `fb522bdd`: **one credit-sale predicate for the whole tree**,
resolving a collision neither sibling lane could see (`F-UTLKVIT-PREDICATE-COLLISION`), plus four pins on
**the round trip through the id a client actually evaluates** — every pin that existed addressed an id read
back out of the journal, which no client ever does.
Held until `D-SPEC-L-UTLKVIT-REPRINT-KIND` is ruled, because re-dispatching it sends an agent at the same
wall.

**What it is blocking**

**The options**

- `forward-the-files`

  - **pro:** the ship-or-stop answer lands the same afternoon, with no token, no signed pilot and no database — and PDF-only is itself a valid STOP answer, so the files cannot fail to answer the question
  - **con:** it is a hand-off only you can do, and the lane sits until it happens
- `onboard-a-venue-first`
  - wait until a real venue completes Tripletex onboarding, then probe entitlement against a live connection
  - **pro:** answers the entitlement half too, which the files alone cannot
  - **con:** no venue is connected today and the integration's own README says the work packages are unbuilt, so this is months, not an afternoon
- `park-alive`
  - leave the lane parked but not deleted until nearer the mandate
  - **pro:** the spike itself argues for this — the sending obligation starts 1 January 2027, so a STOP measured on an August 2026 mix would need reopening almost immediately
  - **con:** onboarding is the module's own stated kill risk and manual price entry is what a pilot venue would quit over, which is why unpark-now was ruled

Ruled: forward-the-files 2026-08-05 by @sven

### D-TRAIN-ERASURE — a frozen name in an append-only table that no erasure request can reach

plan.md:17662

**Why it is open**

Raised by `L-TRAIN-DISPLAY-SNAPSHOT` on hand-back, and it is the reason that lane returned blocked rather
than building. The module's **only** erasure mechanism is the spec's sentence permitting personal
free-text in deviations to be anonymized in place on request. That cannot run on training completions:
the deny-trigger and the append-only guard both refuse an in-place edit.
So the column would create personal data **with no permitted erasure path** and — unlike the
personalliste, which does this exact shape in Workforce — **no retention horizon** after which the
question stops being asked.
This is a fork rather than a lane because all three answers are defensible and they trade different
things: the first spends a C1 exception, the second spends a stated statutory requirement, the third
spends the requirement's other half.
**Correction, 2026-08-03 — the pro recorded against the chosen option was false, and I wrote it.**
`snapshot-with-horizon` was offered on the grounds that the data "dies on a schedule, which is the answer
the personalliste already gives one module over." **It does not.** Measured by the lane sent to build it:
- `RetainUntilUtc` is a **keep-until lock, not a deletion deadline.** Its own test is named *the retention
  horizon is set and cannot be shortened*, and asserts a trigger **refuses** shortening it.
- **There is no sweep.** The field is referenced by four non-test files, all writers and projections.
  **Nothing deletes.** The participant display name is never erased.
So copying that shape would have shipped the defect **with a date next to it**: a frozen name, no erasure
path, and a column that looks like it closed this decision without closing it. The lane built nothing for
exactly that reason.
It also measured the other two groundings and both fail. The Training spec's own §13.5 says retention is
*a documented product policy, not a marketed legal duration — the module never claims a specific statutory
retention period it has not confirmed with counsel*, which is **a written refusal rather than a gap to
fill.** And the personalliste's three-year-six-month period is grounded in bokføringsforskriften § 8-5-6,
the bookkeeping regulation governing the personalliste **as a bookkeeping document** — Training records
are IK-mat, IK-alkohol and HMS, so carrying that period across would invent a duration and attribute it to
a statute that does not say it.
The ruling stands as Sven's; what it was ruled *on* did not survive measurement. See
`D-TRAIN-RETENTION-BASIS`.

**What it is blocking**

- L-TRAIN-DISPLAY-SNAPSHOT — the inspector pack names a person (blocked)
- L-MIG-TRAIN-DISPLAY-SNAPSHOT — the frozen display name the evidence pack reprints (blocked)

**The options**

- `snapshot-with-horizon`
  - **pro:** the pack is stable and the personal data dies on a schedule, which is the answer the personalliste already gives one module over
  - **con:** needs a retention period nobody has ruled, and a sweep deleting from an append-only table is a new exception to C1 rather than an application of it
- `no-snapshot-print-current`
  - **pro:** creates no new personal data, leaves C1 untouched, and has no erasure problem to solve
  - **con:** the internkontroll spec requires the snapshot in two places, and an inspector reading a reprinted pack cannot tell what the record said on the day it was written
- `snapshot-opaque-reference-only`
  - **pro:** satisfies the spec's opaque-identity-reference half and keeps names out of the append-only rows entirely
  - **con:** does not satisfy the display-snapshot half, so the pack still reprints a live-resolved name and the defect survives under a different description

Ruled: snapshot-with-horizon 2026-08-03 by @sven

Reopen when: a retention period is named and an inspector asks for a pack older than it, or the append-only sweep the horizon needs is refused

### D-CONSUMERWEB-WORLD — which ConsumerWeb branch this plan is entitled to read

plan.md:17711

Raised 2026-08-02 while installing the world guards. `../ConsumerWeb` is on `feature/swiss` and one probe
reads it. Writing `feature/swiss` into its `world.config` would have made the guard report conformance —
**by defining conformance as wherever the checkout happened to be sitting.** That is the guard passing by
definition rather than by measurement, so the expected value is left empty and the fact reads `unknown`.
`unknown` is deliberately not `false` here. The checkout has not failed a check; it has never been given
one, and those two states must not render the same.

**The options**

- `declare-feature-swiss`
  - **pro:** it is where the checkout stands and where the consumer work has been happening
  - **con:** this plan is the Norwegian restaurant modules, and a Swiss branch may carry a different product's cart, so the fact would be measured against the wrong thing while reading green
- `declare-a-restaurant-modules-branch`
  - **pro:** one world for the whole program, and the conformance guard then means the same thing in all three repos
  - **con:** no such branch has been shown to exist in ConsumerWeb, so this option may be an instruction to create one rather than to choose one
- `drop-the-probe`
  - **pro:** removes the estate's only unruled cross-repo assumption, and the plan stops claiming a fact it cannot ground
  - **con:** loses the single check that the consumer cart carries the reservation token, which is the Meals guest path's one wire into this plan

Ruled: drop-the-probe 2026-08-03 by @sven

Reopen when: a consumer branch is declared for this program, so the cart probe can be grounded and restored

### D-GROWTH-RETENTION — retention against Growth's own deny-triggers

plan.md:17772

**Why it is open**

- Erasure is **not** blocked. Five Growth tables carry append-only triggers, but the contact-point
  table does not, and erasure nulls the encrypted address there.
- What the triggers block is time-limited retention purging — a contradiction between the spec and
  the schema, not a rights problem.
- Whatever is ruled, C1 is the constraint it has to survive: an append-only table is never purged
  in place.

**The options**

- `amend-13`  **(recommended)**
  - **pro:** no migration and no weakened control; the append-only receipts are kept for the life of the controller relationship
  - **con:** the spec's stated retention windows stop being true and have to be rewritten
- `dated-carve-out`
  - **pro:** honours the spec as written
  - **con:** each trigger has to admit DELETE past a horizon, a materially weaker control needing its own tamper tests
- `aggregate-reduce`
  - **pro:** keeps the evidential value while shrinking the row count
  - **con:** a new summary table plus the same carve-out on the source rows
- `shred-is-retention`
  - **pro:** matches what the code already does, since erasure is a crypto-shred on the contact point rather than a delete
  - **con:** receipt volume grows without bound, and it now grows with mail volume

Ruled: amend-13 2026-07-31 by @sven

### D-MEALS-SPLIT — whether a company pays part of a lunch and the guest pays the rest

plan.md:17828

**Why it is open**

Surfaced by the lane that built the funded checkout. Its objective said the company pays its share and
the guest the remainder; that is not buildable — above the cap the reservation is denied outright, and
nothing in the cart, the completion route or the quote reserves a partial amount. The lane reported it
rather than inventing a shape.

**The options**

- `cap-only`
  - the company funds up to its cap and an order above it is refused before the guest commits
  - **pro:** it is what is built and proven today, the refusal is legible, and no money is ever split across two tenders
  - **con:** an employee who wants a 210-kr lunch on a 188-kr allowance cannot simply pay 22 kr — they order something else or nothing
- `split-tender`
  - the company pays its share and the guest pays the remainder on their own card
  - **pro:** it is what a person expects from an allowance, and it removes the most likely daily friction
  - **con:** the cart carries one payment type, completion takes one token, and the quote reserves a cap rather than splitting one — this is a new endpoint and a second tender on one order, in the module whose money path is the most carefully guarded in the estate
- `topup-wallet`
  - the employee pre-loads their own balance and the company reimburses
  - **pro:** keeps one tender per order
  - **con:** invents a wallet, and Norwegian tax treatment of a reimbursed balance is a different question from a subsidised meal

Ruled: cap-only 2026-08-03 by @sven

Reopen when: a pilot venue reports employees abandoning orders at the cap rather than reordering

### D-CORE-PIN — how a shared-client fix reaches the clients that ship

plan.md:17846

**Why it is open**

`core` is a git submodule and five checkouts hold **four distinct pins across three Core branches**.
ConsumerApp's pin is not even an object in ConsumerWeb's copy, and both carry commits with identical
subjects under different hashes. No single Core commit reaches every client.
The lane established this before changing anything and stopped rather than fixing one copy and
declaring the defect closed — which is the trap that turned a plan fact green over an absent capability
two days ago.

**What it is blocking**

- L-CORE-ORE-LABEL — a price with øre stops printing a suffix that means it has none (built)

**The options**

- `bump-all-four`
  - land the fix on each Core branch and bump the pin in every client repo
  - **pro:** the defect is actually gone everywhere a guest can see it, which is the only version of "fixed" that means anything
  - **con:** four repos, three Core branches, and two of them are divergent local histories carrying commits with identical subjects under different hashes — this is a day of careful work before anything is better
- `consumer-only`
  - fix the two clients that show the defect and leave the others pinned
  - **pro:** it is where a guest actually sees a price, and it is already done and proven
  - **con:** the estate keeps four Cores that disagree about how money is printed, and the next person to read one of them learns the wrong rule
- `converge-core`
  - reconcile the Core branches onto one history first, then fix once
  - **pro:** it removes the class rather than the instance, and the class has now produced two lane-blocking findings in two days
  - **con:** a reconciliation nobody has scoped, on submodules that have drifted for months, before a one-line rendering fix

Ruled: consumer-only 2026-08-03 by @sven

### D-DOCKER-VM — how the SQL tier gets a machine to run on again

plan.md:17889

**Why it is open**

**Recovered without the reset, 2026-08-01.** The agent spent three minutes booting the VM before
discarding anything, on the theory that ext4 would replay its journal now the host had space. It did.
Everything came back readable, and the ruled option was not needed.
That call mattered: a factory reset would have destroyed **nine locally-built images with no registry to
pull them from** — including the harness and stage0 API images — plus five named volumes holding
**seeded harness databases**. Given the known migration-replay bug that breaks a fresh harness bring-up,
rebuilding those was not obviously cheap.
Reclaimed instead: 40.1 GB of build cache, two crash-orphaned test containers and nine anonymous volumes
from the run that died. Docker's image went 66 GB to 35 GB, host free went 53 to 103 GiB, nothing a lane
needs was lost.
**Proven, not assumed:** 18 of 18 SQL-traited tests green across four fixtures and four real containers,
each migrating the full chain from empty. The three migrations authored on 2026-07-31 that had never met
a real database have now run against one four times, and one fixture additionally proved the down-and-up
round trip. The remaining 520 are untested-since, not known-red.
reopen_when: the VM fills again, or a reset is needed a second time — at which point the question is not how to recover but why this host cannot hold the estate's working set
**Corrected 2026-08-01, and the correction changes the remedy.** The lane first attributed this to
Docker's image growing until the host was exhausted. Measured an hour later with that lane idle, the
image had **not grown a byte since the VM died** — and the host kept losing space anyway, swinging
between 30 GiB and 9 GiB free as other lanes build and test. Docker's 66 GB is a *symptom*.
The working set is the estate itself: roughly 122 GB under `~/okam`, 34 GB of system temp, 28 GB of
application support and 23 GB in `/private/tmp`, on a volume all but full. So **resetting Docker reclaims
66 GB once and this host fills again** — it is the wrong remedy, and the option below that says so is
the one to weigh.
**Docker's virtual machine is down and will not come back.** A lane's SQL run died seven minutes in
with every test reporting a terminated connection, after the VM's filesystem logged an aborted journal
and remounted **read-only**. Its sparse disk image had grown to fill a volume with almost nothing left.
So the SQL tier is unavailable estate-wide. Everything authored today that depends on a trigger, a
rowversion or a filtered index — three migrations among them — is proven at the application layer only.
The reclaim is not mine to run: every option either destroys containers I did not create or removes
build output from under a lane that may be mid-compile.
**One measured lead, 2026-08-01, and it is not ours.** Ten gigabytes of the twelve now free sit in
Claude Code session scratch for a *different* project — `raiis-saladin-web` at 5.2 GB and
`raiis-saladin-core` at 4.9 GB under `/private/tmp/claude-501/`. This estate's own session scratch is
241 MB.
If no session is live on that project those directories are dead and removing them nearly doubles the
free space in one command, without touching a container, a worktree or a build. I have not removed
them: I did not create them and cannot tell from here whether a session still holds them.

**What it is blocking**

- L-MRG-WASTE — a reason-coded waste entry survives the frozen week (built)

**The options**

- `reset-docker-vm`
  - factory-reset Docker Desktop, which discards its 66 GB disk image and every cached image and stopped container
  - **pro:** it gives a clean VM in minutes
  - **con:** it destroys eight pre-existing stopped containers and every cached image, none created by any lane here — and measurement since shows the image is not what is filling the volume, so it buys 66 GB once and the host fills again
- `reclaim-build-output`  **(recommended)**
  - delete the 516 obj and bin trees across the estate's worktrees, then restart Docker
  - **pro:** it touches no container and no source, and the estate's own notes say it reclaims tens of gigabytes in minutes
  - **con:** a worktree a lane is compiling in loses its build mid-run, and the same sweep has silently gutted node_modules binaries here before, which needs a forced reinstall to repair
- `defer-sql`
  - keep building on the fast tier and accept that nothing touching a trigger, a rowversion or a filtered index is proven until a machine exists
  - **pro:** nothing is destroyed and lanes keep landing
  - **con:** three migrations and every immutability guard authored today are proven at the application layer only, and that is precisely the gap that has twice let a dropped SQL guard ship

Ruled: reset-docker-vm 2026-08-01 by @sven

Reopen when: the VM fills again, or a reset is needed a second time — at which point the question is not how to recover but why this host cannot hold the estate's working set

### D-BUILDER-PRUNE — how the build cache stops eating the machine again

plan.md:17966

**Why it is open**

**A disk cap would not have helped.** The sparse image fails when the *host* runs out, whatever its
declared maximum — Docker was the victim rather than the cause, exactly as the corrected diagnosis said.
What actually filled the volume was 40.1 GB of build cache accumulating under a policy that is switched
on and not holding.

**The options**

- `scheduled-prune`  **(recommended)**
  - a periodic `docker builder prune -af --filter until=48h`, by cron or once per wave
  - **pro:** it is the fix that would actually have bitten, and it costs a cold first build per lane after each prune — minutes, against the hours a dead VM cost today
  - **con:** something has to own the schedule, and a prune landing mid-build slows whichever lane is unlucky
- `lower-the-cap`
  - drop the builder's keep-storage from 20 GB to 10 GB in the daemon config
  - **pro:** one token
  - **con:** the cap is **already set at 20 GB and the cache still reached 40.1 GB**, so the setting is configured and demonstrably not holding at this build rate — and it only applies on restart
- `accept-and-watch`
  - leave it, and reclaim by hand when the volume gets tight
  - **pro:** nothing to build or own
  - **con:** today that meant a read-only VM, a dead tier, a stalled lane and several hours

Ruled: scheduled-prune 2026-08-03 by @sven

Reopen when: a prune lands mid-build often enough to cost more than the cache did, or nobody owns the schedule

  treats an advance for a mixed-rate proposal, which is a fact about the outside world that this
  plan does not hold. Ask the accountant, then rule.
- What the plan can say: the shipped behaviour is `keep-withholding`, and it is honest rather than
  wrong — the VAT total goes null rather than guessing.
- C6 applies to whatever is chosen: the product may not print a VAT treatment it cannot produce
  the document for.

**The options**

- `on-account-liability`
  - **pro:** the deposit is a customer prepayment on account with no VAT column at all, which is what an accountant expects
  - **con:** five follow-on sub-decisions about rendering, sign and forfeiture
- `taxable-advance-composite`
  - **pro:** one number, taxed at the accepted proposal's composite rate
  - **con:** a composite rate is a fiction when the proposal mixes rates
- `taxable-advance-configured`
  - **pro:** the venue states one rate
  - **con:** needs a schema column and a prompt that does not exist
- `keep-withholding`
  - **pro:** shipped and honest, since the statement's VAT total is null whenever a deposit line is present
  - **con:** every realistic pilot settlement therefore shows no VAT total at all

Ruled: on-account-liability 2026-08-03 by @sven

### D-ACCT-TIMING — fix the missing unique index now, or at the chain squash

plan.md:18074

**Why it is open**

- `F-ACCT-DUP` is a blocker flag, not a warning: the accounting day can post twice today on any
  database built from the migration chain.
- R3 in intent.md is the reason the model-built tier cannot answer this — it agrees with the model
  and never with the database a customer would get.
- Whatever is ruled, C2 binds it: one migration author at a time, and the chain is the truth.
**Settled by measurement 2026-08-03, and it settles the deferral argument outright.** The lane ran
`ef migrations add` against the current model: it produced an **empty `Up` and `Down` and left the snapshot
unmodified.** The snapshot had been regenerated after the model gained the index, so the differ has nothing
left to emit — **the squash could never have emitted these operations.** The two documents that disagreed
about whether it would are now moot; the migration had to be hand-authored, exactly as `hand-author-now`
assumed.
Three further findings from that lane, each worth keeping:
**The generated rollback could never have run.** A typed column alteration resolves its indexes-to-preserve
from the *target* model, so the generated `Down` dropped the unique index twice and re-created it on the
widened column — unique over an unbounded string, which SQL Server refuses outright. **Found by reading the
generated script rather than the C#**, which is the only place it was visible.
**It refuses; it does not repair.** The migration counts duplicate groups and stops. It deletes nothing,
because both duplicates may have reached the webhook and **which claim is real is an accounting decision,
not a schema one.** The sweep queries are recorded as an owner action.
**The catch this makes live was over-broad**, and that mattered the moment the index existed: a bare update
exception would have reported **any** write failure as a safely-skipped duplicate, and the accounting day
would have silently never posted. Narrowed to the unique-violation test.
It also kept the migration number the ledger had already named this change, rather than minting a fresh
one — two entries for one migration is the failure the renumbering convention exists to prevent.

**What it is blocking**

- L-ACCT-UIDX — the accounting day cannot post twice on a chain-built database (blocked)
- F-ACCT-DUP — AccountingSummaries has no unique index in the migration chain · stays open while that lane waits

**The options**

- `hand-author-now`  **(recommended)**
  - **pro:** the accounting day stops being able to post twice on any database built from the chain
  - **con:** takes the single migration-author slot
  - **cost:** needs a duplicate sweep before the index can be created
- `defer-to-squash`
  - **pro:** the squash re-emits model-versus-chain drift in one pass
  - **con:** two live documents disagree about whether it does, and one says the operations must be hand-authored either way

Ruled: hand-author-now 2026-08-03 by @sven

Reopen when: the duplicate sweep the index needs cannot be run against a real database, or the squash is shown to emit the operations after all

### D-PREF-ORIGIN — how the preference centre becomes same-site

plan.md:18117

**Why it is open**

- `F-PREF-UNREACHABLE` records the symptom: the preference centre cannot open a session from the
  deployed origins, so a guest cannot take themselves out of a mailing list.
- That withdrawal path is named in the objective, which is why this is not a cosmetic fork.
**Correction, 2026-08-03 — the brief this was ruled against contained a false "or", and I wrote it.** It
said both the CORS policy and the cookie have to move, *or* the API has to be served same-site. **That
"or" is wrong.** `api.okam.no` and `okam.no` are the same *site* but a different *origin*, so CORS still
applies and the wildcard is still refused. **The named CORS policy is required under both rulings.**
Anyone who read that sentence and shipped only the subdomain move would have shipped a still-broken page.
The lane implemented `api-subdomain` plus the **named-CORS half** of this ruling, and left the cookie at
`Strict`. Its finding on the other half: `samesite-none` would permanently give up the browser's own
cross-site protection, leaving the CSRF token as the sole defence, **to buy what the subdomain gives
free** — and it would still need the same CORS policy. Strictly more change, strictly less protection.
Both can technically stand; usefully they cannot, and the lane recommends retiring the `samesite-none`
half rather than leaving two live instructions. **That is yours to retire, not mine.**

**What it is blocking**

- L-GROWTH-PREFCENTRE — a guest completes a withdrawal at the deployed origins (blocked)
- F-PREF-UNREACHABLE — the preference centre cannot open a session from the deployed origins · stays open while that lane waits

**The options**

- `named-cors-policy-plus-samesite-none`  **(recommended)**
  - **pro:** keeps the API where it is, with a named policy carrying explicit origins and credentials on the preference controller plus a cross-site cookie
  - **con:** adding credentials to the default policy would throw at startup, so the scoping has to be exactly right
  - **cost:** a cross-site cookie is a weaker posture than same-site
- `same-origin-proxy`
  - **pro:** dissolves both halves at once with no policy or cookie change
  - **con:** the proxy in this repo targets a loopback address and describes itself as a preview tool, so this is a deployment decision about hostnames rather than a code change

Ruled: named-cors-policy-plus-samesite-none 2026-08-03 by @sven

Reopen when: the API moves to the same registrable domain, at which point the named policy and the cross-site cookie are both unnecessary

### D-SPEC-L-MEALS-FUNDED — the plan contradicts what L-MEALS-FUNDED observed

plan.md:18163

**Why it is open**

The exit's second conjunct assumes a consumer checkout in this repo; there is none — pages/webshop/checkout.vue is a RedirectToNewStore stub to https://shop.okam.no and no page or component references useCheckout or cartService().Complete, so no capture under artifacts/journeys/ can show a funded order completing here.
The lane also surfaced a defect in this plan rather than in the code. `core/` is a git submodule, and the
two clients pin different lineages — this repo `cd1cc86`, ConsumerWeb `8931bc39`, already 25 and 11
commits from their merge base, with `PaymentType` members that differ. So writing the reservation token
into *this* repo's `cart-service.ts` would turn `fact:meals.token.client` green while the shipped
consumer checkout still sends nothing: a green fact standing over an absent capability, which is what C3
and C5 exist to refuse. Whichever client is ruled, that probe and `F-MEALS-UNFUNDED`'s `clears_when` both
have to move to that client's Core lineage.
Secondary, for whoever writes the client: `CreateMealsQuoteRequest.QuoteHash` has no pinned algorithm —
it is stored verbatim and used only in an idempotency fingerprint — so the first client to bind the quote
invents the hash contract by accident.

**The options**

- `consumerweb`  **(recommended)**
  - bind the funded checkout in ConsumerWeb, the checkout real guests use today
  - **pro:** a green fact then means a guest can actually pay with a company account, which is the only version of this that a pilot can use
  - **con:** a third repo outside this plan's two branches, on feature/swiss, and its Core pin has already diverged from this one
- `consumer-native`
  - bind it in frontend-mono apps/consumer-native
  - **pro:** matches the standing 2026-07-20 ruling that the consumer go-forward client is apps/consumer-native, so the work is not thrown away
  - **con:** the longest path to a funded order anyone can demonstrate, and not what a pilot venue's guests hold in their hands this quarter
- `consumerapp`
  - bind it in ConsumerApp
  - **pro:** reaches app users without touching the go-forward decision
  - **con:** ships a capability into a client the estate has already decided to move off
- `here`
  - build a funded-order surface in Web-modules
  - **pro:** keeps the plan's scope to two branches and there is a precedent, the public Events deposit page
  - **con:** this repo has no cart and no ordering flow at all, so this means building an ordering surface rather than wiring one

Ruled: consumerweb 2026-07-31 by @sven

Reopen when: the ConsumerWeb Core pin is reconciled with this plan's, or the go-forward consumer client changes so that binding funded checkout there is no longer throwaway work

### D-SPEC-L-MEALS-GATE — the plan contradicts what L-MEALS-GATE observed

plan.md:18190

**Why it is open**

**Recommended:** row-not-status — it is what the lane already built and proved, and the honest limit of
what this machine can show. The other two are worth ruling on their own merits, but neither is needed to
unblock the seed.
"`Configure<MealsFeatureSettings>` is called nowhere, so the gate reads false in every deployment whatever configuration says" — the first clause is true and the conclusion is false. Program.cs:813 calls `services.AddMealsFeatureOptions()`, which binds `Features:Meals` via `AddOptions<MealsFeatureSettings>().BindConfiguration(...)`; `BindConfiguration` was chosen over `Configure<T>(GetSection(...))` because `AddServices(IServiceCollection)` has no IConfiguration in scope. So `fact:meals.gate`'s probe (`Program.cs contains:Configure<MealsFeatureSettings>`) cannot go green without writing a redundant or worse binding, and will keep stamping `unconf` at every refresh. Change the probe to `contains:services.AddMealsFeatureOptions();` — that is the one line whose removal darkens the gate, and MealsFeatureSettingsBindingTests already pins that exact string comment-stripped.

**The options**

- `row-not-status`
  - judge the issue call by the deposit row it committed, not by its status code
  - **pro:** measurable today with no credentials at all, and it proves exactly the thing the lane was about — that the flag gate cleared, since the service commits the request and its receipt in the first transaction before it ever reaches the provider
  - **con:** it stops short of proving a guest can pay, so the provider leg stays unproven by this seed and by anything else
- `sandbox-credentials`
  - provision Vipps test-MSN credentials so the seed can reach a genuine 200
  - **pro:** proves the whole leg including the provider, which nothing else on this branch does
  - **con:** needs a credential only Sven can obtain and place, and a sibling review found the initiate sends no required return URL, so a 200 may be unreachable until that lands anyway
- `fake-in-demo`
  - register a substitute deposit port when the demo stack runs
  - **pro:** a demo walks the entire flow end to end with no credentials
  - **con:** the demo then proves the fake works rather than the product — the same fabricated-evidence shape the Meals review flagged, where every green capture test reaches the ledger through a row nobody can produce — and it puts a substitution in the production composition root

Ruled: row-not-status 2026-08-03 by @sven

Reopen when: Vipps sandbox credentials arrive, so the provider leg can be proven rather than reasoned about

### D-GROWTH-EVENTS — how Growth learns a mail bounced, now that Postmark is bound

plan.md:18210

**Why it is open**

Found by `L-GROWTH-MAIL` after the provider ruling landed, not before it. `GrowthWebhookIngestionService`
requires a signature and a timestamp header, and **Postmark does not sign webhooks** — that is documented
provider behaviour, not an oversight. So with Postmark bound, no delivery, bounce or complaint event can be
ingested at all: nothing reaches Delivered, and provider-driven suppression never fires.
This is a consequence of `D-MAIL`, discovered downstream of it. It does not reopen that ruling — the
transactional path is proven live — but it means the ruling bought less than it appeared to, and the
difference is exactly the delivery-truth half.

**The options**

- `basic-auth-url`  **(recommended)**
  - a Basic-auth webhook URL plus an IP allowlist, which is Postmark's own documented answer
  - **pro:** keeps the ruled provider and needs no second vendor
  - **con:** a shared secret carried in a URL is weaker than the HMAC the ingestion path was built for, and the allowlist is an operational thing somebody has to maintain
- `split-provider`
  - keep Postmark for transactional mail, use a signing provider for the bulk stream
  - **pro:** delivery events stay HMAC-verified, and the code already assumes that
  - **con:** two vendors, two data-processing agreements, two places Norwegian guest data lands
- `no-events`
  - accept that the pilot has no delivery truth
  - **pro:** nothing to build, and a pilot of ten guests can be watched by hand
  - **con:** no Delivered state and no provider-driven suppression, so a hard bounce never suppresses and the same dead address is mailed forever

Ruled: basic-auth-url 2026-08-03 by @sven

Reopen when: the IP allowlist proves unmaintainable, or guest volume makes a shared secret in a URL an unacceptable posture

### D-EHF-UNPARK — whether the EHF invoice lane ships before the pilot

plan.md:18232

**Why it is open**

**The fact that changes this:** Norway's B2B e-invoicing mandate was approved by parliament in
June 2026 — EHF issuance mandatory from 1 January 2027, reception and digital bookkeeping from 2030.
From next year essentially every supplier invoice a Norwegian restaurant receives exists as
structured line-level XML.
The whole category's invoice-OCR apparatus — xtraCHEF, Craftable, MarketMan — is a workaround for
unstructured paper. EHF makes that workaround unnecessary here and nowhere else. `MarginEhfInvoiceParser`
is already written, 954 lines against EN16931, and deliberately unreachable: a test pins that it has
zero production callers pending this ruling.
Journal-exact sales in, mandate-exact purchases in. That is the pair no imported competitor can copy
without rebuilding for Norway.

**What it is blocking**

- L-MRG-EHF-SPIKE — ~~a real venue's invoices are classified and the ship question is answered~~ (retracted)

**The options**

- `unpark-now`  **(recommended)**
  - run the Lane 0 spike against a real venue's invoices, then wire it
  - **pro:** it converts the module's second-worst deal-loser into the only structural advantage nobody imported can copy, and the parser is already written and green
  - **con:** pre-mandate, some suppliers still send PDFs, so the spike may find the input is not yet structured enough to rely on
- `after-pilot`
  - leave it parked until a venue is using the module
  - **pro:** the pilot answers whether costing is wanted at all before we spend on how prices arrive
  - **con:** onboarding is the module's own stated kill risk, and manual price entry is what a pilot venue would quit over
- `never`
  - accept manual and CSV price entry as the product
  - **pro:** nothing to build
  - **con:** every competitor demos snap-a-photo invoice capture in the first meeting

Ruled: unpark-now 2026-08-03 by @sven

Reopen when: the spike finds supplier invoices are not structured enough to rely on before the mandate

### D-GR-DEADLINE-CALENDAR — which calendar the article 12 deadline is read on

plan.md:19546

**Why it is open**

**Recommended:** venue-local — it is the only option where the printed date is the date the venue is
actually held to.
**This ruling gates more than it looks.** The statute lane established that **both** remaining counting
rules wait on it. The weekend half of the working-day extension needs no data at all — but *is the due day
a Saturday* **has no answer until you know which calendar it is read on.** And rounding to the last moment
of the due day, which sounds like a pure improvement, **would move the printed date a day later for every
row east of UTC** — the dangerous direction applied universally instead of to a handful.
The public-holiday half is separate and is **not implementable honestly**: the Regulation defines holidays
as those designated in the Member State where action is taken, which is per-market data **the product holds
for no market.**

**The options**

- `venue-local`
  - compute and render the deadline on the venue's own calendar, date-only
  - **pro:** it dissolves the mismatch entirely, and it is the reading a venue would defend to a regulator, since the obligation is theirs and the day is theirs
  - **con:** it needs a venue timezone the module does not currently carry, and two venues in different zones would see different deadlines for requests filed in the same instant — which is correct and will still look like a bug
- `utc-both-ends`
  - keep computing on UTC and render on UTC too, labelled
  - **pro:** one calendar end to end, no new data, and the arithmetic already verified exact stays untouched
  - **con:** a Norwegian venue reads a deadline in a timezone it does not live in, and the label is the only thing preventing a misread
- `utc-compute-local-render`
  - what ships today
  - **pro:** nothing to do
  - **con:** **the two disagree by a day in a narrow window, in the direction that grants headroom the statute does not** — a request filed just after local midnight at certain month-ends

Ruled: venue-local 2026-08-03 by @sven

Reopen when: two venues in different timezones need one deadline, or the venue timezone the module now carries turns out not to be reliable

### D-MRG-PRICE-CORRECTION — how a frozen week is repriced, and who is named for it

plan.md:19571

**Why it is open**

**Recommended:** backdated-correction — it is the only option where the corrected week actually costs
correctly and the price book stops lying about what was charged.
**But the attribution is not optional and that is why this is a ruling.** A backdated correction removes
the premise an existing refusal is written on. **The lane found the column has nowhere to live:** the price
row carries no actor, the import batch requires a file hash under a unique index, and **Margin has no audit
ledger at all** — which is plausibly the same question as the open Growth ledger decision.
**Executed 2026-08-03, and the `con:` was handled rather than absorbed.** The ruling made false the premise
an existing refusal rested on — *a wrong price is superseded forward, never withdrawn.* The lane
**re-grounded that refusal at all five sites carrying it**, on what the write does to money already
reported, and made the re-grounding **executable**: a symmetry test drives both money doors and asserts the
two refusals **agree**, so drift on either side reds.
A frozen week now reprices by exactly the amount the forward path refuses in that same world, with the
prior revision still finalized at its old figure. **The bound is that a correction is permitted only where
a strictly later price exists**, so it always closes at a real successor boundary — proven non-vacuously by
showing the forward path *accepted* in the identical world.
**Two errors it caught in itself and corrected rather than narrowing the claim:** a wire test that passed
without reaching the module (see `F-401-UNREACHABLE-OVER-HTTP`), and closing-instant logic that handled a
null predecessor but not one closing *past* its successor — found by self-review **after** a green tier.
**On the backfill question it declined to inherit a sibling's reasoning**, which is the right instinct: this
is an existing table rather than a new one, but the column is nullable **by design rather than by
concession** — manual and imported rows legitimately have no corrector, so a not-null column would be
semantically wrong however many rows existed.
**One judgement call left explicitly for whoever authors the column.** The lane **deliberately skipped a
stage flag** for the correction endpoint: the flag catalog is a shared surface with three flag lanes in
flight, and this cannot merge before the column exists anyway.
The consequence, stated rather than buried: **the endpoint is live the moment the column lands**, unless
somebody decides otherwise. It is recorded here so that is a decision rather than a discovery.

**What it is blocking**

- L-MRG-PRICE-CORRECTION — a frozen week can be repriced when a later price already exists (blocked)

**The options**

- `backdated-correction`
  - an operator-only backdated price that closes into the timeline, bounded so it can never become the open row
  - **pro:** **no money is edited**, the correction is a first-class row with its own source, and it costs **exactly one column**
  - **con:** it needs that column and therefore a migration into a contested chain, and it **removes the premise an existing refusal rests on** — the import approval refuses an unattributed actor *on the grounds that a wrong price is superseded forward, never withdrawn*
- `statement-override`
  - a per-statement price override on the correction revision
  - **pro:** it touches the price book not at all, so the timeline keeps saying exactly what a supplier charged when
  - **con:** **a table plus an override map threaded through the calculator, the resolver and the memo key** — and **it still leaves the price book wrong for every later week and every later read**
- `leave-it`
  - accept that a frozen week cannot be repriced once a later price exists
  - **pro:** nothing is built and the timeline stays inviolate
  - **con:** **the correction revision silently reproduces the identical wrong cost forever**, and the control that appears to offer a correction does nothing

Ruled: backdated-correction 2026-08-03 by @sven

Reopen when: the import approval refusal cannot be re-grounded once superseded-forward stops being the reason, or the column is refused by the chain

### D-SPEC-L-UTLKVIT-REPRINT-KIND — the plan contradicts what L-UTLKVIT-REPRINT-KIND observed

plan.md:19695

**Why it is open**

Both halves are already closed at the base the brief itself sends me to, and the second half's prescribed remedy is harmful. Half 1 ("BuildReceiptAsync derives the kind from entry.ReceiptType ALONE") was true at lane/utlkvit-replay-source 3a509b68, where the brief was filed; L-UTLKVIT-SALE-ROW then added the third forward resolution in BuildDocumentForAsync, so at any base carrying BOTH lanes the SALREC of a credit sale already reprints as the utleveringskvittering through GET /pos/receipt/{id}, the print endpoint and the public page. Half 2's stated consequence ("a client reprinting from the natural field gets the wrong paper") is therefore false for the same reason: model.JournalEntryId is the sale's id, and the sale's id now resolves forward. Half 2's remedy - move JournalEntryId onto the delivery entry so the model "addresses it in the field a client actually reads" - would BREAK the register: FinalizeService.FinalizeReturnAsync refuses any original whose ReceiptType is not Sale, and RefundModal.vue calls RefundCash(receipt.journalEntryId), so a credit sale would become non-refundable at the till. Sale-row's choice (JournalEntryId stays the sale's; the sale resolves forward on read) is the correct one and must not be undone. Corrected exit, which I built: keep the field pointing at the sale and pin the ROUND TRIP on the id the register actually hands the client, since every pre-existing pin addresses an id read back out of the journal instead.

**What it is blocking**

- L-UTLKVIT-REPRINT-KIND — a credit sale reprints as an unmarked sales receipt (built)

**The options**

- `take-the-corrected-exit`
  - keep JournalEntryId pointing at the sale, and pin the ROUND TRIP on the id the register actually hands a client
  - **pro:** it is built, and its four pins address the expressions a client evaluates rather than an id SELECTed back out of the journal, which is what every prior pin did — deleting the forward resolution reds all eight
  - **con:** the flag's original wording, "the model addresses it in the field a client actually reads", stays unsatisfied on paper and has to be rewritten
- `move-the-field-as-briefed`
  - put the delivery document's id in JournalEntryId
  - **pro:** the model then addresses the handover document directly, which is what the flag asked for
  - **con:** it makes a credit sale NON-REFUNDABLE AT THE TILL — the return path refuses any original whose receipt type is not Sale, and the refund modal calls straight through that field
- `move-the-field-and-widen-the-return`
  - do the above and teach the return path to accept a delivery original
  - **pro:** both halves, no lost capability
  - **con:** it widens what the refund path accepts inside kassasystemforskrifta territory, which is a much larger change than the defect justifies, and it removes a refusal that is currently load-bearing

Ruled: take-the-corrected-exit 2026-08-03 by @sven

Reopen when: the return path is widened to accept a delivery original, at which point moving the field stops costing till refunds

### D-WOLT-HOSTED-EXEMPTION — whether the Wolt menu sync stays exempt from the hosted-service floor
